title: Transits
summary: How a planet you cannot see shows up as a dip in a star's light, and what the dip tells you.

badge.name: Dip detective
badge.text: You can read a planet's size and orbit from its transit.

links.label: Fold a real light curve in the hunt lab
How this site's pipeline finds dips

steps.heading: A dip in starlight
body: We cannot see a planet many light-years away. But when it passes in front of its star, it blocks a little of the star's light. A graph of brightness over time, called a light curve, shows a dip. This is a transit.

facts.text: A planet passing in front of its star slightly dims its light, which shows up as a dip in the light curve.

checks.quote: the planet passing in front of its star ever so slightly dims its light
the light curve will show a dip in brightness

steps.heading: The depth tells the size
body: The fraction of light blocked is about the planet's area compared with the star's: (planet radius ÷ star radius) squared. So the depth tells you how big the planet is compared with its star.
Earth crossing the Sun would block about 84 parts per million. Jupiter would block about 1%. Small planets make tiny dips, which is why they are hard to find.

facts.text: The depth of a transit is about the square of the planet-to-star radius ratio (Winn 2010, Eq. 22).

checks.quote: the relative dimensions of the planet and its host star

facts.text: The size of the planet can be calculated from how much the star's brightness drops.

checks.quote: the size of the planet itself can be calculated based on how much the star’s brightness lowered

facts.text: Earth crossing the Sun would block about 84 parts per million; Jupiter about 1%.

steps.heading: Repeats give the orbit
body: One dip on its own could have many causes. Dips that repeat on a fixed schedule give the planet's period, the time it takes to go around once. From the period you can work out the size of the orbit.

facts.text: The size of a planet's orbit can be calculated from its period.

checks.quote: The size of the exoplanet’s orbit can be calculated from how long it takes to orbit once (the period)

questions.prompt: Two planets cross the same star. One makes a dip 4 times deeper than the other. How do their sizes compare?

choices.text: The deeper one is 4 times wider
choices.explanation: Depth goes with area, not width.

choices.text: The deeper one is 2 times wider
choices.explanation: Depth goes as the square of the size ratio, and 2 squared is 4.
A deeper dip means more light is blocked.

questions.explanation: The depth is about (planet radius ÷ star radius) squared, so 4 times the depth means 2 times the width.

checks.quote: the relative dimensions of the planet and its host star

questions.prompt: About how many parts per million of the Sun's light would Earth block in a transit?
questions.explanation: (Earth's radius ÷ the Sun's radius) squared is about 84 parts per million.

questions.prompt: What gives you a planet's orbital period?

choices.explanation: Depth tells you size, not period.

choices.text: The time between one dip and the next
choices.explanation: The planet comes back once per orbit.
Brightness alone says nothing about the orbit.

questions.explanation: Dips repeat once per orbit, so the time between them is the period.

checks.quote: how long it takes to orbit once (the period)
